title: Council Post: Why Applications Built On Top Of GenAI Will Deliver AI's Value
text:
CEO and co-founder of Automation Anywhere, a leading global provider of enterprise process automation.
Everyone is eager to discuss the topics of artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI and large language models (LLMs). It makes sense, as today’s LLMs represent a significant technological shift in AI that will reshape companies, industries and the world.
The wide availability of pretrained generative AI models in 2023 broadened the range of challenges that can be addressed through technology. However, modern LLMs and generative AI chat apps alone are not where the real benefit of this technology will ultimately be found. It will be in the more complex applications built on top of LLMs—those capable of running end-to-end processes without supervision—that will make the largest impact across consumer and enterprise markets.
History Of Disruption
If we consider how technological advancements have disrupted the market over time, the core technology innovation itself often isn’t where the real value lies. Instead, it’s in the application layer built on top, where the technology can be customized and fine-tuned to address large problems that exist in a specific industry or business.
Consider personal computers, which came to market in the 1970s. It wasn’t until the first spreadsheet computer program—VisiCalc—was introduced for the Apple II in 1979, followed shortly by 1-2-3 for the IBM PC in 1982, that interest in personal computers took off. To this day, the software applications that run on top of PC (and now mobile) hardware are what drive value and function for business and consumer users.
Similarly, the web gained widespread popularity with browsers like Mosaic and Netscape and service providers like America Online in the early 1990s. The browser wars followed, along with a substantial surge in investment in internet-based companies. Although the commercialization of the internet has had its periods of boom and bust, we continue to see the most significant value derived from the web through the services built on top of it, like e-commerce.
We will see a comparable pattern of initial invention and interest followed by rapid innovation of applications and the adoption of generative AI technologies.
Future Of Generative AI
Today’s LLMs provide the building blocks for practical generative AI in the enterprise, but LLMs will not single-handedly solve the challenges that organizations face.
LLMs offer deep banks of information and value, but they don’t act on that information in complex ways, and most of the current applications built on them have limited enterprise use. Ask ChatGPT, Google Gemini or Microsoft Copilot how to run an audit, and they will provide a simple path forward based on existing information and best practices. But these tools can’t then turn around and run the audit for you.
This is why large action models (LAMs) might prove to be the killer applications of the generative AI era.
LAMs are AI systems designed to carry out tasks within computer applications that humans would ordinarily handle, allowing business processes to run without human intervention. They can take the information generated and distilled by LLMs and turn it into something actionable to the benefit of the enterprise, substantially accelerating process times to enable more agile and efficient operations.
Early use of LAMs has been more consumer-facing, where simple chat-based interactions allow AI to take actions with minimal training, including actions that the model may never have seen before. For instance, the Rabbit r1 device, which launched at CES in 2024, runs on an LAM-based operating system to execute verbally requested tasks, including booking flights or streaming movies.
That said, enterprise-grade LAMs already exist and can be implemented by organizations today. For example, one of our customers is using a combination of AI and automation—also called “intelligent automation”—to streamline its client experience and administrative support process by automating its clearing house (ACH) transactions.
In these examples, AI makes independent evaluations of proper courses of action, then initiates processes, actions, content and changes based on those decisions, all to optimize a multistep process. This is where the next generation of generative AI will shine.
Challenges Of LAMs
All great technology, especially when new, brings benefits as well as challenges. LAMs hold enormous potential for enterprise benefit through generative AI, but it’s also important to acknowledge the difficulties of adopting them today. Here are a few to consider:
1. The models require significant compute capacity that is not casually available. The cloud is a solution, but this can pose challenges from both a regulatory perspective and in the ability to make LAMs available in smaller devices without internet connectivity.
2. Letting the LAM take actions without control is still an uncomfortable proposition. Governance is mandatory, but experience is also required. Knowing how to automate a broad range of applications and having an established track record will be key.
3. Models today do not reason well when planning against a goal and adapting to changes as they complete steps. For example, if we ask a model to accomplish a goal that requires many steps, it will use what it has seen as common approaches to reach that goal, but it cannot logically identify if a particular step is missing or out of order. Many are working to strengthen this ability in upcoming generations.
To help address many of these challenges in the short term, an intermediate step could be connecting LLMs to process automation. This offers the flexibility to interface with humans naturally while maintaining control over the business process that is executed.
Conclusion
We are in the very early stages of the most disruptive technology of our lifetime. The excitement around LLMs and generative AI is entirely justified as the technological foundation supporting and shaping the future of work. But it’s just the beginning.
I look forward to the evolution of this conversation as the adoption of applications—LAMs and their corresponding use cases—gains steam and organizations begin to realize the full potential of generative AI across the enterprise. The killer apps of AI are emerging.

title: What To Know About G42—The Emirati AI Giant That Just Got A $1.5 Billion Investment From Microsoft
text:
Topline
Microsoft on Tuesday announced it will invest $1.5 billion in leading United Arab Emirates artificial intelligence firm G42, the tech giant’s latest high stakes investment in the sector and a sign of growing ties between Washington and Abu Dhabi as the U.S. fights to stay ahead of China in the race to control AI.
Key Facts
G42 is a technology holding company and a giant in artificial intelligence, forming a crucial part of the UAE’s plans to become a world leader in the field with a variety of companies in areas including biotechnology, surveillance, healthcare and data centers.
The firm has strong connections in the region and is chaired by one of the most powerful members of Abu Dhabi's royal family and UAE national security adviser Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, as well as backed by Emirati sovereign wealth fund Mubadala.
Since its founding in 2018, G42 has has partnerships with major firms such as OpenAI, Dell, IBM, Microsoft, Nvidia and Oracle, Cerebras, which is building G42 a super computer, pharma titan AstraZeneca, genetics giant Illumina and Mercedes.
In recent months, G42’s ties to China have come under close scrutiny in the U.S. amid growing security concerns and fears the connections could compromise American technology.
The Emirati company has since severed its links with Beijing and the New York Times reports the latest deal with Microsoft places a series of protections on the AI products shared with G42 and has an agreement to remove Chinese equipment from its operations, including Huawei telecoms equipment.
Microsoft vice chair and president Brad Smith, who will gain a seat on G42’s board as part of the agreement, told journalists the deal had been made in “close coordination with the governments of both the UAE and the United States” and that Washington had offered Microsoft “strong encouragement… to move forward in this process.”
Crucial Quote
When asked whether the deal with Microsoft was a reward for G42 cutting ties with China, CEO Peng Xiao told journalists the deal was more about what the company could do rather than what it wouldn’t. “I would focus on our decision to form this partnership with Microsoft to really develop our capabilities on a global scale. Less focus on what we choose not to do.”
News Peg
The deal expands an existing partnership between the two firms and gives Microsoft a minority stake in the company. In return, G42 will run its AI services and applications on Microsoft’s cloud computing platform, Azure, which is sensitive and regulated technology, and collaborate with the U.S. firm to bolster the safety and security of its infrastructure. According to Bloomberg, G42 made a secret pact with the U.S. to divest from China before making the deal with Microsoft. According to the Times, its deal with the tech giant will include implementing measures to protect Microsoft’s AI technology, particularly regarding Chinese gear, and give Microsoft the power to audit how G42 uses its technology. Both companies also said the partnership will support the development of a skilled AI workforce for the UAE and broader region, including a $1 billion investment in a development fund for developers, and see them collaborate to build AI and digital infrastructure across the Middle East, Central Asia and Africa. Sheikh Tahnoon said the “investment in G42 marks a pivotal moment in our company’s journey of growth and innovation” and signifies “a strategic alignment of vision and execution.” It is a “testament to the shared values and aspirations for progress, fostering greater cooperation and synergy globally.”
Key Background
Microsoft’s deal with G42 is the company’s latest big swing in the AI space as companies like Google and OpenAI compete for talent and access to key technologies. For Microsoft, this includes training workers for an AI-enabled future, a $10 billion deal with ChatGPT maker OpenAI and a partnership with French AI startup Mistral. The U.S. giant’s pivot to AI also includes a keyboard design change, the first major alteration to the hardware in decades. The new design features a dedicated button to summon its AI assistant, Copilot.
What To Watch For
The Times reports a second phase of the deal is possible but not yet negotiated. It could be controversial, the Times said, as it may include the transfer of some of Microsoft’s AI technology.

title: SAP BrandVoice: How AI Can Get Railways On Track For Transformational Growth
text:
Modern railway systems operate a complex network of vehicles, tracks, and infrastructure that’s prime for disruption from the latest batch of AI innovations, including generative AI. That’s because AI-fueled technologies are peerless at accomplishing data-driven tasks that address this industry’s foundational reason for being, namely the safe, efficient, and on-time delivery of goods and passengers in compliance with country and regional regulations.
In a series of recent in-depth conversations, leaders from some of the world’s leading railways shared how traditional and generative AI technologies can help their organizations address their biggest challenges. After reading the report, I caught up with Johann Schachtner, who leads solution management for transportation asset management at SAP.
“While many railway operators are concerned that the scope and readiness of their current systems may be too complex to support AI-based capabilities, they are very interested in exploring how these advances can build resiliency for growth,” said Schachtner. “Railway operators realize that infrastructure and rolling stock breakdowns anywhere impact the entire business. In fact, echoing many of the people we recently talked with, one operator said that the cost of failure was so large that the gains realized through AI will be significant.”
Dynamic railway maintenance with AI
Railways are undergoing tremendous expansion in some regions as well as modernization of aging infrastructure in others. AI is well-suited to keep pace with the industry’s brisk growth and ambitious plans. In their candid dialogues, rail transport leaders ranked dynamic maintenance among the top places where AI can make a difference.
Railways have long used AI-based visual image recognition on diagnostic cars to spot track defects, allowing operators to identify potential problems and proactively take maintenance steps for greater efficiencies. With insights from real-time data, railways can more cost-effectively allocate and manage materials, people, and equipment within dynamic maintenance windows. AI-based data insights can help railways shift maintenance from fixed preventive to breakdown reduction through predictive and prescriptive activities.
It's early days for generative AI, but potential areas for maintenance-related advancements are emerging. Generative AI tools could quickly collect and analyze structured and unstructured data across the railway ecosystem, for example from OEM partners. Coupled with IoT-based augmented or virtual reality technologies, generative AI could surface data for technicians in the field to speed up diagnostic and preventive maintenance. Functioning as a virtual assistant, the technology could draw from a variety of relevant sources including historical equipment data and manuals to provide the fastest and safest fix for specific issues.
AI guides more informed decision-making
Industry leaders are just as interested in AI’s potential to help orchestrate project management across miles of equipment and infrastructure along railway lines. Using AI-fueled ‘what if’ scenario planning that incorporates variables from hundreds of projects, operators could adjust maintenance and inventory management plans to reduce costs and improve service levels. They could also strategically align investment decisions with evolving organizational priorities including safety, regulatory compliance, and growth.
People-centric efficiencies from AI-powered asset performance management
Paradoxically, bringing advanced AI-based tools into daily railway operations creates a human-centered workplace. These capabilities can deliver up-to-the-minute notifications, recommendations, and predictions that help people meet daily and long-term responsibilities. For example, using insights from connected data between maintenance equipment, station facilities, depots and yards, safety and security systems, and IT, people can manage and improve the lifecycle of railway assets, reducing downtime while increasing performance and value.
“Our SAP Business AI strategy is designed to provide customers with relevant, reliable, and responsible AI from real-time data that’s integrated across the business including maintenance, supply chain, HR, procurement, sales, and finance,” said Schachtner. “We’re embedding our AI copilot Joule into our cloud-based applications portfolio, which aligns with railway industry demands around enterprise asset management. AI-based tools will provide people with the updated information they need to make more informed decisions faster for business benefit.”
AI heralds positive railway disruption
Railway transport tends to grab market attention only when disruptions occur. AI technologies promise to deliver a good kind of disruption for an industry undergoing rejuvenation for the next era of economic growth.

title: AI Is Creating An Influx Of Child Sex Abuse Images, Data Shows
text:
The mainstreaming of AI image generators has brought with it an influx of artificial child sexual abuse imagery, according to a new report from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.
The nonprofit—a go-between that funnels information about suspected CSAM and child sexual exploitation from tech and social media companies to law enforcement globally—received 36.2 million such reports to its “CyberTipline” in 2023, up from north of 32 million the year prior and more than double the pre-pandemic volume in 2019. Of those 36.2 million, NCMEC determined almost 5,000 to be the result of generative AI, though it says the actual count is likely considerably higher.
“It's fairly small volume when considering the overall total of the CyberTipline reports, but our concern is that we're going to continue to see that grow, especially as companies get better at detecting and reporting,” Fallon McNulty, director of the CyberTipline at NCMEC, told Forbes.
“What is really scary for us is, if we think about just the scale: It's so small and already has made such a huge impact,” she added.
Over the past year, there has been a pronounced uptick in reports of AI image generators being used to create illegal sexual abuse images. Deepfake nude photos of students are roiling middle and high schools across the United States. Some of the most popular new AI tools on the market have used illegal CSAM to train their models. And prosecutors recently charged a man in one of the first criminal cases involving AI-generated CSAM.
“The scale of this could explode.”
Recently, a small-but-growing group of generative AI shops have begun to cooperate with NCMEC to track and flag apparent CSAM, McNulty said. Leading the charge is OpenAI, creator of ChatGPT and text-to-image generator Dall-e, which started engaging with NCMEC last year and is now appearing in its report for the first time. Anthropic and Stability AI have also joined the effort, McNulty added, which is starting to paint a clearer picture of how most of this content is being made—whether by inputting text prompts, for example, or by using AI to manipulate photos of children or known CSAM. Although the biggest social media apps are being used to spread it (and roughly 70 percent of tips related to AI CSAM were submitted by mainstream platforms), ground zero is often open source models or off-platform, McNulty said. Some reports that NCMEC has received from social media companies include posts, comments, hashtags or chat logs detailing what AI model had been used.
With AI developing so rapidly and proliferating so quickly, McNulty said she fears “the scale of this could explode”—further inundating a disperse law enforcement system already struggling to keep up. That it is becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish fake AI-generated CSAM from the real thing is another challenge. And although a handful of big generative AI players have agreed to work with NCMEC, some of the smaller platforms often reported to the organization— like apps that can “nudify” a photo, for example—have not, McNulty noted.
The trend continues—in the first quarter of 2024, NCMEC has seen roughly 450 reports a month of CSAM stemming from AI—and is only expected to grow.

title: Council Post: Who Really Owns AI Art? What Businesses Need To Know About Generative AI And Intellectual Ownership
text:
Cathy Ross, the finance and tech expert behind Fraud.net's AI-powered risk management platform.
The world entered a new era when OpenAI released ChatGPT on November 30, 2022. The chatbot went viral and became a household name. Less well-known but equally disruptive are DALL-E, Stable Diffusion and Midjourney, text-to-image generators released in 2021 and 2022. Heralded by some as a great equalizer, these tech tools provide even non-artists opportunities to create masterpieces. However, others have sounded the alarm.
Generative AI systems are trained by mining the internet for images and language, using human endeavors to create something new, and potentially very lucrative. Naturally, questions arise over usage and ownership: Who is benefitting from the proceeds of sales? Can someone claim an AI-created piece of art as their own if it is influenced by someone else’s work? What if it’s been created using hundreds, or even thousands, of other people’s art?
Creative types using others’ work to inform their own is nothing new. Whether you call it taking inspiration from, borrowing, building upon or straight-up stealing often depends on how much of the original work is recognizable in the finished piece.
Generative AI has added more layers to an already complex issue. DALL-E, for example, is an artificial neural network—similar to how the human brain functions—that learns by analyzing and connecting many datasets. So, that piece of work it spits out based on a text prompt may draw from masters like Rembrandt, Van Gogh and Picasso. It could also be mirroring sources closer to home, like your neighbor who posted her illustration on her socials or maybe even you.
Here's what creators and business leaders need to know about the evolving nature of AI art:
The Current Legal Landscape For Generative AI
In our increasingly AI-dominated world, issues of copyright and ownership are being fiercely contested in living rooms and courtrooms. In fact, lawsuits are piling up.
Getty Images filed two lawsuits against Stability AI for copyright infringement in the United Kingdom and the United States, claiming millions of its copyrighted images, text and meta-data were unlawfully used to train Stability AI’s Stable Diffusion image generator. They seek damages of up to $150,000 per infringed work. If they win, that could mean a potential payday of $1.8 trillion.
In another case, a group of artists brought a class-action lawsuit against Stability AI, Midjourney and DeviantArt for copyright infringement last year. They claimed some images created with those companies’ AI tools mimicked their style without permission or compensation. A judge dismissed the charges against Midjourney and DeviantArt, but allowed the suit against Stability AI to continue.
In 2023, German photographer Boris Eldagsen shed some light on the pitfalls of AI-generated art when the piece he submitted to the Sony World Photography Awards won in the creative open category. He later revealed it was not made with a camera and refused the prize, explaining that he entered the competition to test if competitions are ready for AI entries. Eldagsen has since called for open discussions on the very definition of photography.
While generative AI has implications for all types of business, advertising and marketing firms may be especially vulnerable to its hazards. This technology makes creating new logos, brochures and other sales and marketing collateral exponentially faster and easier. But as the above cases suggest, these systems come with caveats when using an unknown dataset.
Generative AI And Risk Management
Underlying data also poses risks to financial services and fraud protection, especially anti-money laundering compliance. The new technology has already positively impacted these sectors by helping to automate onerous operations, alleviate human error and reduce the number of false positives that arise in other financial monitoring software. However, as Dr. Mario Menz, global head of risk and compliance for BVNK, writes (paywall), “AI systems are only as good as the data they are fed.” In his column for Compliance Week, he points to privacy and security concerns as well as biases in training datasets stemming from systemic discrimination. The argument is that centuries of societal prejudices and behavior will inevitably show up in coding unless guardrails are put in place. In other words, ethical, legal and social concerns exist in every arena where generative AI exists.
The Business Response To Generative AI
Current laws surrounding copyright and fair use may need updating as they face legal challenges from creators. A recent challenge decided by the Supreme Court in 2023 did not involve AI, but could indicate how courts may rule in the future. In Andy Warhol Foundation for Visual Arts, Inc. v. Goldsmith, the Supreme Court ruled in favor of plaintiff Lynn Goldsmith. At issue was Warhol’s "Orange Prince," which appeared on a Vanity Fair cover and was based on a photograph of the musician taken by Goldsmith for Newsweek. The Court found that Warhol’s work did not constitute fair use as it served the same commercial purpose as the original photograph.
It’s safe to say the art world, much like the written word, will never be the same. Some organizations are banning the use of AI-generated art; the scientific journal Nature announced last summer that it will not allow its use in images and video. But other companies are embracing the new technology, even if they have been burnt by it. They see a path forward to an equitable future. Getty Images began offering a service allowing customers to create unique AI images based on its substantial archive of photographs and images. CEO Craig Peters said that the service “wasn’t trained on the open internet with stolen imagery” and that artists would be compensated for their work.
Compensation (i.e., economic security) and recognition are two basic human requirements. Whether in art or business, we want to be appreciated, to get credit when it’s due and to earn a commensurate amount for our efforts. If humans and generative AI are to coexist peacefully, programmers and tech corporations would do well to code that lesson into the machine.

title: Council Post: Catalyzing Supply Chain Transformation: The Role Of Artificial Intelligence In Oracle's ERP Solutions
text:
Dipak Kulkarni is an IT Director at Crenlo and has an excellent command of solving various business problems by offering IT solutions.
Oracle's Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) application is widely recognized as a leading solution for supply chain management, bolstered by sophisticated tools like Oracle Advanced Supply Planning (ASCP). This software suite efficiently gathers crucial data pertaining to master data and supply-demand snapshots, providing valuable insights and generating actionable suggestions such as new orders, rescheduling options or cancellations for both work orders and purchase orders. Should the planning process operate daily, these suggestions and exceptions are churned out every day, reflecting the dynamic nature of supply chain management.
In practical terms, a company of modest scale (typically with annual revenue under $300 million and comprising about three sites with an inventory of approximately 60,000 items) generates a significant volume of suggestions. I've found it's not uncommon for such a setup to produce over 500 suggestions for buyers and upwards of 300 for planners.
Addressing these recommendations demands a considerable allocation of resources. Buyers must engage with suppliers to adjust orders, while planners are tasked with coordinating operational activities and resolving any quality issues with materials. This intensive process often necessitates daily hours-long internal meetings dedicated to troubleshooting issues related to receiving goods and supplier payments.
However, the sheer volume of suggestions, coupled with the intricacies of supply chain management, can render the manual execution of these tasks an unrealistic endeavor. Even with an expanded workforce, the potential for human error looms large, posing significant challenges to operational efficiency and accuracy.
Building Effective AI Models: From Data Analysis To Integration
In response to these challenges, harnessing the power of artificial intelligence (AI) emerges as an alternative solution. AI, characterized by its ability to simulate human intelligence in machines, offers a transformative approach to supply chain management. By emulating human thinking and learning processes, AI systems are adept at performing a wide array of tasks traditionally associated with human intelligence. These include problem-solving, natural language understanding, pattern recognition and decision-making, all of which are integral to effective supply chain management.
The integration of AI into the supply chain ecosystem represents a paradigm shift. However, implementing such a solution requires a strategic approach and careful planning. In particular, modifications to existing systems, such as Oracle ASCP, are necessary to accommodate AI functionalities seamlessly.
One crucial aspect of this integration involves the creation of a concurrent program within Oracle ASCP. This program serves to store historical data, ensuring that valuable information is preserved before plan data is purged upon completion of actions by planners or buyers. This historical data serves as the foundation for AI model development, providing essential insights into past trends and patterns.
To build an effective AI model, historical data must be meticulously analyzed and processed. This involves preprocessing steps such as handling NULL records and ensuring data uniformity. Once the data is prepared, various AI models can be developed and tested to identify the most effective approach. Promising models are then converted into application programming interfaces (APIs) for seamless integration with existing systems.
The implementation of AI-driven decision-making represents a significant departure from traditional approaches to supply chain management. Rather than relying solely on human judgment, AI systems are capable of autonomously executing suggestions and exceptions on behalf of users. This not only reduces the burden on human resources but also helps minimize the risk of errors and delays.
Initially, AI capabilities may be restricted to "B" or "C" class items, where the risk of late delivery or excess inventory is relatively low. As the AI model gains trustworthiness and reliability, its scope can be expanded to encompass a broader range of items and scenarios.
In addition to streamlining operational processes, AI-driven solutions offer a host of indirect benefits. By automating routine tasks and decision-making processes, users can focus their time and energy on strategic initiatives and exception management. This can help enhance productivity and build trust in the system over time, fostering a culture of innovation and continuous improvement.
Although AI paired with the Oracle ASCP solution is ideally suited for managing supply chains, it encounters certain limitations. AI operates on a data model tailored to specific data sets. However, when supplier-specific circumstances shift—such as alterations in contract terms or material shortages due to external factors like labor strikes, machinery downtime or unforeseen natural disasters—the response from suppliers changes, necessitating revisions to the AI model.
Similarly, changes within the planner or buyer organization responsible for implementing these adjustments can lead to deviations in actions from what the AI model has been trained on. Therefore, ongoing optimization is essential, preferably on a weekly (if not daily) basis.
In Conclusion
While Oracle Cloud offers AI solutions with cloud applications, the transition from on-premise applications like Oracle EBS to the cloud represents a significant undertaking for many manufacturing companies. Moreover, Oracle continues to support EBS applications, making it important to develop AI solutions that are compatible with existing systems.
I believe the integration of AI into supply chain management represents a game-changing initiative for businesses. By strategically harnessing the power of AI, organizations can aim to unlock new levels of efficiency, accuracy and innovation, driving tangible business results and staying ahead in today's competitive marketplace.

title: Council Post: From Coding Grind To Innovative Mastermind: Our Teams’ Transformation
text:
Tomas Smalakys is a CTO of NordPass, password management solution for businesses and consumers, developed by Nord Security.
As the CTO of a rapidly growing cybersecurity company, I've seen my fair share of technological advancements come and go. Some were revolutionary game-changers, while others were just overhyped instances that fizzled out faster than a kid's interest in a new toy. But I can say with certainty that artificial intelligence falls firmly into the former category.
When I first started hearing the buzz around AI a few years ago, I'll admit I was skeptical. Having been burned by failed "next big things" in the past, I approached it with cautious optimism. But as I saw the tangible ways it was already impacting industries far and wide, from healthcare to finance to manufacturing, I knew this wasn’t a passing trend.
For my engineering teams specifically, integrating AI into our workflows has been a game-changer, unlike anything I've seen before. We're saving countless hours on tasks that previously bogged us down while unlocking new levels of creativity and problem-solving capabilities. Simply put, AI is a force multiplier that's supercharging our productivity and innovation.
And it’s not just me. According to a GitHub study, 92% of U.S.-based engineers working in large companies reported using an AI coding tool. Such stats are hardly surprising, given the significant benefits AI can offer engineering teams, enabling them to tackle more significant challenges and solve complex problems more effectively. The time and brainpower AI frees up for my engineering teams is allowing them to unlock new levels of creativity and problem-solving abilities. Let me give you some specific examples of the tools that have been game-changers for us.
Unleashing Creativity And Efficiency With AI
One area where we've seen massive time savings is in code generation and optimization. Tools like GitHub Copilot and Tabnine use AI to autocomplete code and suggest relevant snippets in real life, as my engineers are writing. It saves a truly tangible amount of hours compared to manually looking up syntax, configurations, parameters and all those little nitty-gritty details we need to remember. Our teams can now blast through that mundane stuff and focus purely on the higher-level logic.
Testing and debugging workflows have been revolutionized, too, thanks to AI assists like DeepCode and Amazon CodeGuru. In the past, a lot of us have experienced writing code thinking we nailed the solution, only to have it fail once implemented because of some blind spot we missed. With these AI tools proactively catching potential issues beforehand, so much time is saved by addressing problems earlier in the cycle before they compound.
Onboarding new engineers is infinitely easier now as well. Engineering teams can now use tools like SourceryAI to instantly generate clear documentation and explain any complex segments of our codebase. This makes the ramp-up period so much smoother for fresh team members or those joining from other squads. No more spending weeks just trying to decipher previous devs' spaghetti code!
The time saved from intelligently documenting and surveying our codebases is immense, but perhaps even more impactful is how AI is augmenting our actual problem-solving process. With Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT and other advanced AI assistants, my engineers can rapidly find relevant information, proven solutions and expert insights on any technical challenge we're facing. Rather than everybody constantly reinventing the wheel, we can build directly upon the cumulative knowledge of the entire field.
And then there are powerhouse tools like Refactor.AI that actually optimize and restructure our existing code while preserving core functionality. This keeps our products running lean, mean and free of accumulating technical debt over time. Needless to say, maintainability becomes easier in such a context.
Fostering Creativity And Personal Growth
But beyond just the code itself, AI is empowering my teams to spend more time on the "human" elements of their craft. Things like leadership training, professional development, interpersonal skills, mentoring and a lot more. We now have breathing room for those often neglected aspects of work that are so vital yet constantly get deprioritized when you're stuck in the dense jungles of execution.
At the end of the day, AI is enhancing my engineers' abilities as creative problem-solvers and well-rounded professionals. We're upskilling and evolving right alongside the advent of these amazing technologies that are propelling our industry forward.
So, for any technical leaders out there who have been hesitant to fully embrace the AI revolution, I urge you to take the plunge. The potential upsides are immense in terms of team productivity, innovation and overall human flourishing. Just be ready for your best people to start surprising you with creative solutions you never could have anticipated. That's the real power of empowering your teams with the time and mental freedom AI can provide.

title: Council Post: Harnessing The Power Of Generative AI For Your SMB
text:
Ken Pomella CEO RevStar.
As a serial entrepreneur, I know firsthand how challenging it can be to find competitive advantages that can catapult your business to the next level. While these efficiencies might feel few and far between, I believe that generative AI, when used strategically, can help many small- and medium-sized businesses improve their current practices.
Understanding The Benefits Of Generative AI
In a world where businesses are struggling with rising wages and scarce talent, generative AI is presenting a transformational opportunity for many organizations. As the founder of a technology consulting firm, however, I find that most SMB leaders are not actively considering this route, possibly due to the AI drama playing out with the tech giants, the overwhelming prospect of implementing such advanced technology into their operations or potential challenges of the technology to consider.
However, with the right approach, I believe AI is accessible to small- and mid-sized businesses. Many companies that have moved forward with this strategy are already seeing results. According to a 2023 study commissioned by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and conducted by Teneo Research, 91% of business owners using AI reported that it helped their businesses operate more efficiently. A similar percentage further stated that AI has helped them find new customers, improve their customer communications and grow in challenging conditions.
Furthermore, generative AI can help smaller companies compete on a significantly larger scale. That same U.S. Chamber of Commerce study found that 75% said AI helped them compete with much larger firms. In a 2024 Harvard Business Review article, Oguz A. Acar and Andrés Gvirtz argue that point even further. They believe AI can level the playing field between small and large corporations, allowing small entities to compete with the gigantic budgets of the largest competitors.
How To Implement AI Into Your Business
Many people hesitate after experimenting with ChatGPT and other mostly free offerings. AI is still evolving and is by no means perfect. In fact, it is still quite messy, so you do need to be cognizant of the risks as well.
One significant challenge is dealing with "hallucinations." These are instances where AI generates false or misleading information. This phenomenon can pose risks, especially when AI is used for content creation, data analysis or decision-making processes, potentially leading to inaccuracies or misinformation that could harm your business's credibility or profits.
Another challenge comes from ethical and privacy concerns. AI critics and watchdogs have focused on the sources AI has been trained on, as well as the potential for bias in AI-generated outcomes. As a business using AI, you must tread carefully, ensuring that how you implement the technology aligns with ethical standards and respects customer privacy and trust.
On the technical side, SMBs venturing into the generative AI space may face other obstacles. That’s why it’s critical to allow sufficient time for development and even more time for careful testing.
What many tentative SMB leaders often don’t realize is that once these challenges are realized and overcome, generative AI can have significant advantages, even with a learning curve. One of the biggest obstacles at this point is that many people don't know where to start.
In my company’s experience helping firms implement AI successfully, enterprising SMBs are harnessing AI’s potential best in the following areas.
• Marketing and promotions.
• Customer service and communicating with customers and prospects.
• Identifying potential customers.
• Managing inventory.
• Handling administrative processes.
To expand on this point, here are two real-life success stories where small businesses have used AI to achieve notable results.
Transcending Automation
For creative agency Corpora Studios, the time-consuming task of photo editing was sapping their team’s energy and taking away from other productive uses of time. The team worked with an AI consultant to modify an existing AI photography editor to meet their specific needs. They trained the AI on what adjustments they normally needed and had the AI learn the style and preferences of each photographer. The result was about 96% less editing time and an 83% reduction in costs.
Increasing Personalization
By integrating AI-powered chatbots into its website, electric bike company Blix dramatically improved the personalized assistance available to website visitors. The AI chatbots were trained to answer questions and help customers choose the products that would best meet their needs. This increase in personalization helped increase both sales and customer satisfaction, contributing to a 150% increase in revenue in one year.
Four Tips To Harness The Power Of AI
In my experience, possibilities begin to emerge once you take the first step. Once you've declared that you're initiating an AI effort, follow these steps to get started.
1. Identify the "sticking points" in your business.
What tasks seem to require an inordinate number of resources? Also, look at frustrations. What areas hold your company back? Then, look at where your team is least efficient. These all can be potential areas where AI might be able to make an impact.
2. Research existing AI tools.
AI tools are entering the market at a breakneck speed, so it always makes sense to see if something off the shelf can help. Today, many tools and platforms offer a gateway to the powers of AI without the development or infrastructure price tag. While these may not be the ultimate answer, they can sometimes be a solid start.
3. See if outside experts can help you maximize your results.
Bringing in outside expertise makes sense when you're serious about having AI transform your business and lack the necessary expertise within your organization. While there is typically an upfront cost, AI consultants can help shortcut costly trial and error and get AI working for you much faster.
4. Empower your team to embrace AI.
In SMB ecosystems, adding AI is not about replacing humans but empowering them to do more. Help cultivate curiosity and learning around AI. Sponsoring AI skill development and career progression among staff members can pay off in the long run, encouraging team members to look for opportunities to further harness AI's remarkable capabilities.
Key Takeaways
It's not often that such a transformative approach becomes so widely available to companies of all sizes. Although there are still wrinkles to be ironed out when it comes to the current state of AI, I believe a thorough strategy can help overcome any challenges while improving the practices of many organizations.

title: The 2024 Sustainability Priority List
text:
Over the last year, supply chain leaders faced an array of challenges, including high interest rates, labor shortages, supply constraints, and an uncertain geopolitical environment. On top of that you can add sustainability related factors such as resource scarcity, climate change impacts, and increased regulatory pressures. It was a trying year. The challenges will continue into 2024 and beyond, making this a crucial moment for sustainability and supply chain leaders. With many organizations also looking at cost-cutting measures, those leaders will have to find ways to achieve sustainability goals while juggling varied demands of the market and the organization. However, through innovation, collaboration, and in some cases, redefining outdated processes and operations, organizations can address these headwinds while staying committed to critical sustainability objectives. Here are a few key areas to consider as we look ahead:
Carbon transparency will be in high demand
In 2023 several pieces of legislation, both state and federal, that were focused on increased carbon reporting requirements were brought forward. The SEC’s climate disclosure rule mandates standardized carbon emissions reporting for publicly traded companies, with new disclosure rules for Scope 1 and 2 emissions going into play as early as 2025. It takes time to establish emissions reporting processes to meet these new requirements. This is particularly true for complex rules like those pertaining to Scope 3 emissions reporting in California, which requires companies active in the state and generating $1 billion+ in revenue annually to start reporting in 2026.
Therefore, planning and preparation to ensure organizations are equipped to meet these standards should be a priority for leaders this year. These increased regulations will also make organizations’ sustainability profiles more visible to their regulators, stakeholders, and consumers. For example, starting in January 2026, importers of carbon-intensive commodities in Europe – such as iron, steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, electricity, and certain derivatives of these products – will have to pay a 'carbon tax' in the form of CBAM certificates purchased on an official platform. Failure to comply with reporting requirements may impact an organization’s brand and result in severe consequences, such as suspension, revocation of their CBAM registration, a ban on importing goods into the EU, and criminal sanctions.
Companies that fail to report and comply with the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) also face fines of up to 10 million Euros or 5% of their annual revenue. With these significant penalties at play, it’s critically important for organizations to be transparent in their ESG reporting and prioritize their sustainability efforts.
This is where technology can play a key role. One of the challenges when it comes to understanding sustainability performance and making impactful progress is gathering and organizing the required data, which often comes from multiple disparate systems, prone to multiple errors such as duplicates, gaps, and inconsistent formats.
This new formal sustainability reporting environment will require that the core enterprise systems that run organizations must embed sustainability directly within LOB functions such as finance, procurement, supply chain, manufacturing, and human resource operations. Only then can organizations readily analyze sustainability metrics and drill back into the underlying transactional data needed to drive impactful decisions. The message is embed, automate, and capture information, and then use that information in real-time to improve sustainability related performance.
Navigating global disruptions
The impact of climate change on supply chains continues to be an unfortunate reality. In 2023 alone, the drought in Panama slashed the number of vessels able to travel through the canal. This caused delays and pushed some traffic to be offloaded onto rail cars to make the journey across the country before being loaded back onto vessels in the Pacific to continue the journey. Simultaneously, geopolitical tensions in the Red Sea caused shipping rates to skyrocket, and much of that traffic had to be shifted around the Cape of Good Hope. That diversion added roughly 3,500 nautical miles to the journey and produced a significant increase in carbon emissions. The additional financial pressures caused by increased shipping rates and longer timelines put many organizations in a position to make decisions focused on alleviating those costs, without considering the sustainability impacts. However, that doesn’t have to be the only way.
With robust data, route alternatives and scenario planning in place, decision makers can weigh sustainability impacts in near real time, rather than just focusing on financials. This enables organizations to navigate disruptions effectively while balancing costs, timelines, and other factors alongside sustainability concerns. The ultimate question is, how can organizations get to this point where nimbleness, efficiency, and effectiveness collide?
For starters, organizations need to ensure the right tools are in place to obtain and analyze data to inform better decision making and identify opportunities to reduce climate impact. One of the key capabilities needed to address these types of disruptions is effective scenario planning. After all, it’s not a matter of if a drought or other major disruption might hit a key port or trade route, it’s when, and where. Carbon emissions should be factored into strategies for alternative routes so decision makers can see the full picture and weigh sustainability impacts when assessing rapidly changing supply chain conditions.
Not only does that crucial information need to be available to supply chain and sustainability leaders, but they also must be empowered to make sustainability-driven decisions and understand how to strike the right balance between financial and sustainability goals. This requires sound guidance from leadership to emphasize that sustainability is important to the organization and that emissions implications should be factored into decision-making across the company.
Implementing AI for a more sustainable supply chain
While AI (what we now may call “classic AI”) has long been part of many business systems, 2023 was the year when AI truly hit the popular mainstream with the release of ChatGPT and other Large Language Models. Many organizations are looking to 2024 to be the year of execution, when they start reaping the benefits of classic AI and increasingly of generative AI. One area where AI can help in the supply chain is by identifying lead time trends and anomalies to better assess their potential impact. This gives supply chain leaders the opportunity to optimize lead times with more efficient transportation routes and schedules, reducing the carbon emissions generated by transportation activities. Another interesting use case for generative AI that can impact sustainability is the standardization of language across systems that can unify formatting to reduce inconsistencies and errors. Standardizing language and formatting can lead to more efficient communication among various stakeholders involved in the supply chain, ultimately helping to optimize processes and of course, reduce waste.
Between the global disruptions, increased regulation, and rapid advancements in AI, there has never been a greater need for transparency and nimbleness in the supply chain, but there has also never been a greater opportunity to positively impact carbon emissions globally. The decisions made and technologies implemented in 2024 may very well define the sustainability trajectory of organizations for years to come, with the potential to catalyze substantial progress for the business and the environment as we work toward a greener future.

title: Truth In The Signal: Veritone Shepherds New Epoch Of Enterprise Empowerment
text:
By: Christos Makridis
"It’s a brother’s story in many ways," begins Ryan Steelberg, CEO, president, and co-founder of Veritone, reflecting on his unexpected journey from a pre-med student at UCLA to a tech entrepreneur. “It’s those two classic roles you think of in tech startups; me primarily being the front line as the public-facing business leader, and Chad always the technology and product wizard.”
Steelberg stands today as a pioneering force in the burgeoning field of AI software and services, primarily for enterprises and major customers like ESPN, CBS and the US government- but also attainable to mid-sized firms as well. His entry into the tech sphere was marked by a collaborative effort with his brother Chad, a partnership fueled by their shared curiosity and passion for technology, bolstered by steady encouragement from their parents along the way, growing up in Orange County, California. Their journey would ultimately redefine the contours of digital advertising, and eventually, establish key pillars of today’s enterprise AI solutions industry.
The brothers’ first formal internet outing was launching a first of its kind real estate platform in 1994 (akin to what we know today as online real estate listing services), similar to Zillow or Trulia. A big idea for sure, but what appealed most to VCs was the potential to monetize ads across its real estate sites. "Within three months, we had signed contracts with multiple real estate brokerages, including Coldwell Banker, Edina Realty, and Century 21 Realty, generating high demand for advertising space," Steelberg recalls, highlighting the rapid success of their venture. This led to the duo's initial breakthrough with the establishment of AdForce, which became the world's largest centralized independent ad-serving and management solution. Under the Steelberg’s leadership, AdForce pioneered and grew their advanced advertising platform signing dozens of industry behemoths, including AOL and Yahoo, which ultimately lead to an acquisition by CMGI for more than $500 million after going public on Nasdaq in 1999. In 2000, AdForce won the Smithsonian Award for the Best Technology in IT.
Despite a big splash right out of the gate, the Steelberg brothers’ entrepreneurial journey, however, was not without its share of challenges and setbacks. Their next venture in 1999, Winfire, Inc., faced formidable monopolistic obstacles amidst the rapid proliferation of broadband technology. Winfire aimed to provide free high-speed Internet access to broadband users and was established as a DSL (Digital Subscriber Line) service provider, offering an alternative to traditional high-priced paid Internet services. The company had tremendous initial interest, quickly amassing a major paid customer base; however, a breakdown occurred with Winfire’s partnered telecom companies’ ability, or willingness, to deliver timely service, as they instead chose to prioritize existing customers over Winfire’s. It ultimately led to the collapse of the firm, which only had a total lifespan of about a year. “A big early lesson in resilience and dealing with monopolies for two guys in their early twenties”, said Steelberg. “An experience that was definitely formative in seeing all sides of the coin not far out of the starting gate, and ultimately, looking back, it was painful, but there was serious learning there.”
In 2002, the Steelbergs co-founded dMarc, at the time, the largest centralized radio advertising network and digital automation company servicing more than 4,600 Radio Broadcasters. dMarc was acquired by Google in February 2006 for $102 million in cash, with revenue targets that pushed the deal upwards of $1.2B. As of January 2009, total payouts exceeded $400 million. In 2007, the brothers founded Brand Affinity Technologies, an influencer technology and marketing services company.
It was within the crucible of these early adtech-centric ventures, ripe with experimentation, that Ryan honed his skills in navigating the intricate terrain of data-intensive environments and making sense of non-linear content—a skill set that would prove priceless in the field of artificial intelligence, where large language models and engines must effectively analyze tremendous amounts of disparate information and extrapolate faces, logos, trends, patterns, which can then be actioned in myriad ways. Since the essence of adtech lies in the ability to harness vast troves of data and extract actionable insights to optimize advertising strategies, Steelberg’s skill set seamlessly translated into the domain of AI for enterprise.
Human-Centered AI: Redefining Industries
Veritone, which means “truth in the signal,” was launched in 2014 where Steelberg would serve as president from 2015 to 2022 prior to becoming CEO. Again, they began with a core mission of addressing fundamental advertising problems, like the way audio data was ingested and analyzed. Quickly, Veritone's proprietary cloud-agnostic solution, aiWARETM—which can be thought of as an operating system which AI programs are built on—represented a quantum leap in the field, heralding a paradigm shift in the way enterprises interacted with data. Leveraging multiple AI engines in parallel, Veritone's platform offered novel accuracy in analyzing and interpreting audio data.
“The problem we tackled emerged when things shifted from the desktop to your mobile phone,” said Steelberg of Veritone’s beginnings. “When you started to watch a video there was no place to serve an ad adjacent to the content anymore, so we became obsessed with trying to understand native-based advertising or product placement, embedded into the content. It could be the broadcast host for a sporting event talking about Geico during a timeout, it could be a logo of a Chevy truck in a Michael Bay movie, or it could be the Apple laptop on the coffee shop counter in a sitcom. It was this incredibly rich content opportunity where frankly people are most in tune and engaged, and we knew we could figure out a way to look at this more transactionally, meaning could we start to bring structure to linear unstructured audio and video and unlock a world of new possibilities. That was the initial idea,” he concluded. From there, this initial vision of ingesting and understanding unstructured data leveraging AI, would be the foundation for aiWARE and Veritone into the future.
Wth a focus on talent acquisition, media, entertainment, the public sector, and generative AI, Veritone carved a niche for itself, redefining how industries harness the power of AI to drive efficiency, enhance decision-making, and ultimately, maximize human potential. At the core of Veritone's ethos lies a deep commitment to human-centered AI solutions. Unlike traditional approaches that seek to replace human effort with automation, Veritone believes in augmenting human capabilities. With aiWARE, Veritone orchestrated a symphony of machine learning models, transforming raw data into actionable intelligence across a spectrum of industries, just as Steelberg had envisioned.
In the realm of talent acquisition, Veritone's solutions are reshaping the landscape. Veritone Hire seamlessly integrates global job distribution tools with programmatic advertising AI technology. By optimizing recruiting strategies, reducing costs, and improving efficiency, Veritone helps organizations attract diverse talent at scale, reaffirming their commitment to diversity and inclusion in the workplace. Its suite of solutions for talent acquisition cater to both centralized and decentralized recruitment needs and is built on job distribution software and technology specializing in programmatic advertising. Talent acquisition teams and staffing firms can automatically post job ads to job boards, search engines and social media channels all in one place with seamless integrations into over 100 Applicant Tracking System (ATS) partners and optimize individual ads or full campaigns with AI to maximize ROI by increasing candidate volume while reducing wasted ad spend. Veritone enables streamlining of the screening processes by leveraging conversational AI to engage and screen candidates post-apply, all within an ATS.
Veritone's impact extends beyond corporate corridors into the realms of media, entertainment, sports, and broadcast. Their AI solutions empower content creators, advertisers, podcasters, and producers to unlock human potential. From metadata extraction to AI-powered digital asset management, Veritone is disrupting content creation and distribution, providing proof-of-performance metrics, and maximizing the value of every piece of content. Customers can gain value from video, audio, images, text and data through metadata extraction, and search and visualization, enhancing customer support and system integrations. Veritone holds that while generative AI is already used to create outlines, jumpstart content writing and develop ad copy, it will eventually provide an ability to create multilingual content at scale, helping brands test new regions with ad promos and other AI-generated assets and such as full prebuilt campaigns.
“It is in the public sector where we see possibly the greatest growth opportunity in the near term,” said Steelberg. “Where efficiency and safety are paramount, Veritone's AI solutions are making a tangible difference,” he added. Through aiWARE, law enforcement agencies, government bodies, and public safety organizations streamline previously manual processes while gaining invaluable insights from vast amounts of data. Biometric identification means law enforcement agencies can authenticate users and identify callers and suspects by recognizing voices and faces in videos, images and calls. Redaction capabilities help departments save time and costs while freeing up valuable resources by using automating the exaction of sensitive information within audio, video and image-based evidence. Transcription and translation functions enable legal and contact center teams to automate manual work with near-real-time transcription and translation of any data source, while person-of-interest tracking tracks persons of interest across video files regardless of source without using personal identifiable information (PII).
Ethics and Responsibility: Guiding Principles
Veritone remains at the forefront of innovation through the lens of its “AI For Good” motto. Through frequent collaboration with regulators, industry leaders, and stakeholders, Veritone is shaping the future of AI regulation, ensuring that technology evolves responsibly and ethically. With a keen eye on emerging trends and challenges, Veritone is committed to empowering industries to harness the full potential of AI for the betterment of society. “We have a big responsibility here to self-police in this industry in a way that we just haven’t seen in tech, and with the rapid evolution of AI and its profound potential, companies have to lead the charge here,” said Steelberg. “Social media platforms are still trying to play catch up and we see the friction there; it’s a great lesson in how our industry can and must stay ahead of the curve of where this is all going from a societal protection standpoint.”
Veritone has specifically focused on transparency in the design of ethical AI. Their solutions are designed to be easily explainable, generating outputs that are reliable and understandable, in hopes this will build trust among users, stakeholders, and the broader community. Trust is further bolstered by the company's commitment to fairness and non-discrimination, as its systems are engineered to mitigate bias and uphold fairness in their outcomes. The company adheres to stringent security and compliance practices to safeguard data and complies with industry regulations and standards. But as a serial entrepreneur with a passion to empower other innovators, Steelberg is maybe most bullish on the democratization message:
“Fundamentally, we are democratizing and advancing AI access and utilization for enterprises,” Steelberg said. “However, small businesses must also have the tools and opportunity to embrace AI. To avoid the next digital divide—one where I believe the stakes are even higher than ever—small businesses must embrace and educate themselves on AI. Thankfully we have solutions like Veritone’s aiWARE and other cost-effective platforms out there that ensure CEOs can start their AI journey cost-effectively and intelligently. This is a dynamic and ever-changing AI environment that we are living through, and Veritone will continue to build solutions to make AI more accessible and actionable for all enterprises. We see ourselves as ‘wilderness guides for AI’ in a digital world,” he concluded.

title: Council Post: Adversary Or Ally: When Generative AI And Cybersecurity Collide
text:
Dr. Amit Sinha is CEO of DigiCert. Prior to DigiCert, he was President of Zscaler.
There’s an old truism in security that no defense can ever be 100% impenetrable. Rather, the goal is to make it more expensive to breach a target than that effort is worth. From this perspective, then, it’s easy to see why generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is already having a profound impact on cybersecurity.
GenAI is about making it faster, cheaper and easier to perform tasks traditionally handled by human beings. Unfortunately, launching cyberattacks is no exception. With the ability to generate working code and ultra-realistic content in seconds, sophisticated threats that required months of effort from well-funded teams can now be developed automatically, in minutes, and deployed at scale.
The good news is that, even as AI makes cyberattacks more powerful and automated, we can apply the same technology—and the same adjectives—to cyber defenses. Let’s take a closer look at how generative AI is changing the threat landscape and some techniques the security industry is adopting to turn the tables on the threat.
Scoping New Threats
If you’re surveying today’s threat landscape, it’s not hard to see how large language model (LLM) chat clients, image generators and other AI tools can turbocharge existing threats, as well as unleash new ones. As we develop new strategies to protect against AI-driven attacks, some of the biggest areas of concern include:
• Deepfake Attacks: A few minutes on social media will demonstrate how good AI content generators have gotten at creating hyper-realistic forgeries of text, images, audio and video. This means it’s becoming easier for bad actors to spread misinformation, counterfeit identities, propagate scams and erode public trust.
The potential damage from such attacks is hard to overstate. Imagine an ultra-realistic fake video of a world leader announcing a military invasion, a celebrity committing a crime or a corporate CEO declaring bankruptcy. We have already witnessed the impact of fake bank executive videos and AI-generated content, which raises significant concerns about the potential for misinformation and manipulation on a global scale.
• Ultra-Sophisticated Phishing Attacks: Phishing attacks target the most vulnerable part of any system—human beings—by impersonating a trusted entity to trick people into divulging sensitive information. With generative AI, it’s now possible to develop more convincing attacks more quickly.
These can range from the simple (such as impersonating well-known corporations in mass phishing emails) to the complex (like mimicking the writing style or voice of an IT administrator’s boss to trick them into granting access to protected systems). As generative AI advances, these attacks will only grow more realistic and common.
• AI/ML Manipulation: As more organizations depend on AI for daily business operations, machine learning (ML) models themselves are an increasingly attractive target. Attackers can manipulate a target AI by creating false or adversarial inputs to make it less effective. If not detected, such attacks could undermine the effectiveness of important AI-driven systems (such as by spoofing facial recognition against criminal databases or misdirecting autonomous vehicles) and lead to serious consequences.
• Advanced Adaptive Threats: Adaptive malware that changes its behavior to evade detection is already among the most pernicious threats. Fueled by generative AI, emerging malware strains will be even better at assessing the defenses arrayed against them and continually generating more sophisticated versions of themselves.
Harnessing The Power Of Generative AI
Of course, the same attributes that make AI so attractive to bad actors will also benefit emerging cybersecurity defenses. AI can not only unleash a new generation of more effective and adaptive cybersecurity technologies but also help us better address human vulnerabilities.
On the technology side, generative AI can improve threat detection capabilities by providing more granular, comprehensive baselines of system behavior to identify suspicious activity more quickly. AI can also continually incorporate new information—like the behavior of threats observed elsewhere—and adapt an organization’s cyber defenses and security policy in response much more quickly than human operators. GenAI tools can also conduct ongoing, automated penetration testing to identify new vulnerabilities at speeds and scales previously impossible.
On the human side, as attackers use generative AI to quickly develop highly convincing phishing attacks, organizations can use AI tools to conduct more realistic simulations and training. LLM chat clients can help people learn advanced cybersecurity techniques and technologies more quickly, using intuitive, natural language-based queries. And for expert cybersecurity professionals, AI-enabled tools and reporting will only empower them to work more quickly and capably.
Separating Truth From Fiction
Many of the biggest security challenges posed by generative AI involve verifying the authenticity of what you’re looking at. When practically anyone can create sophisticated content and code with a simple query, how can people pick out what’s real from an ocean of fakes? The only solution is to develop new approaches to content trust. Fortunately, the industry is already making advances in this area.
In 2021, a group of leading global technology and media companies formed the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) with the goal of developing an open technical standard to help content creators, publishers and consumers verify the provenance of digital content.
The standard provides a tamper-proof mechanism to attach origin information to media, along with any changes made to it, using the mature digital signature and public key infrastructure (PKI) frameworks that organizations already use to establish trust for users and devices. C2PA has now released version 1.3 of the standard, and many of the world’s biggest technology and media companies (including Microsoft, Intel, the BBC, The New York Times and dozens of others) are working to expand its adoption and use.
Looking Ahead
We’re still at the beginning of the AI-in-cybersecurity story, and it’s hard to conceive all the ways that generative AI could enable new types of threats. Fortunately, the cybersecurity industry isn’t new to this game.
Technologies may change, but professionals in this space have decades of experience studying emerging threats and using every tool at our disposal—including generative AI—to effectively respond to them. By staying vigilant, adapting to new information and working across industries to strengthen content trust, we can build a safer, more secure digital world.

title: Startup Rivos raises $250 million to develop RISC-V AI chips - ET Telecom
text:
- Internet
- 2 min read
Startup Rivos raises $250 million to develop RISC-V AI chips
"RISC-V doesn't have a (large) software ecosystem, so I decided to form a company and then build software-defined hardware - just like what CUDA did with Nvidia," said Lip-Bu Tan, founding managing partner at Walden Catalyst, one of Rivos' investors.
By Max A. Cherney
Chip startup Rivos said on Tuesday it raised $250 million in a funding round that will enable it to manufacture its first server chip geared for artificial intelligence.
Nvidia's combination of chips and CUDA software dominates the market for AI-related computing, and Nvidia gobbled up more than 80% market share of AI chips in 2023. But a host of startups and chip giants have started to launch competing products, such as Intel's Gaudi 3 and Meta's inference chip - both unveiled last week.
Rivos is tight-lipped about the specifics of the product, but has disclosed that its plans include designing chips based on the RISC-V architecture, which is an open source alternative to the architectures made by Arm, Intel and Advanced Micro Devices. Instruction set architectures such as RISC-V are the building blocks of semiconductor designs, and using the open source alternative means Rivos does not have to pay a license fee to Arm.
"RISC-V doesn't have a (large) software ecosystem, so I decided to form a company and then build software-defined hardware - just like what CUDA did with Nvidia," said Lip-Bu Tan, founding managing partner at Walden Catalyst, one of Rivos' investors.
Santa Clara, California-based Rivos is in the process of designing a server chip that combines a central processing unit and AI accelerator component that will be optimized for large language models and data analytics. The company began with the software necessary to compile computer code to allow the chip to run a program and designed the processor around the software.
"Usually the chip companies do it the other way: build the silicon, and then build the software on top," CEO Puneet Kumar told Reuters in an interview. "We decided, as a company that we should first look at software."
Matrix Capital Management was the largest investor in the funding round that also included investments from Intel, MediaTek and Dell Technologies.
